title: Check yourself: substitution and abstract classes

blocks.text: Questions on what this page has just taught. Choose one answer for each.

questions.stem: A `Square` class extends `Rectangle`, and code written for any `Rectangle` gives wrong results when it is handed a `Square`. Which pitfall from this page does that design fall into?

options.says: The page's fourth pitfall: a subclass must be usable wherever its base class is, without altering the program's correctness.

options.text: Forgetting to call the superclass constructor
options.says: That pitfall is about initialising the superclass's state, not about a subclass breaking code that uses the base type.

options.text: Overriding a method with a different signature
options.says: That pitfall is about a method that fails to override at all; here the subclass is used, and misbehaves, in place of its base class.

origin.section: Common Pitfalls and How to Avoid Them

questions.stem: `Shape` is declared `abstract` and has a public constructor `Shape(String color)`. What happens to the statement `Shape s = new Shape("red");`?

options.text: It compiles, and calling calculateArea() on s fails at run time
options.says: The page says an abstract class cannot be instantiated at all, so no object s is ever created.

options.text: It compiles, since having a constructor lets the class be created
options.says: The page says abstract classes can have constructors to initialise common state for subclasses, and still cannot be instantiated.

options.text: It does not compile, since such a class cannot be instantiated
options.says: The page: abstract classes cannot be instantiated; their constructors only initialise state for subclasses.

concepts: An abstract class cannot be instantiated, even though it may declare constructors for its subclasses.
A subclass must be substitutable for its base class without altering the program's correctness.
